title: Wire routing and Bezier controls
summary: Shape connections with independent handles, keep selected controls visible, move selected nodes together, and preserve layouts on the device.
body: These controls are available in the updated Windows source and the device web editor built from the same firmware source. Older installed firmware must be rebuilt and flashed before its browser interface gains the new controls. The Android APK does not gain them merely by updating this documentation.

Highlight and inspect a wire

  1. Open Logics and move the pointer over a connection. Its highlight identifies the wire you are about to edit.
  2. Hovering a wire reveals its routing dots. Hovering an individual dot reveals only that dot’s two existing handles and guide lines.
  3. Click a dot to select it. Its handles stay visible when you move away, so you can reach a distant control. Hovering another dot temporarily shows that dot’s controls; selecting it switches the active dot. Unselected dots stay hidden away from their wire. Controls also stay visible while dragging.

Add and move routing dots

  1. Left-click a wire at the place where you want a bend. This inserts a routing dot in the connection order.
  2. Drag the dot to move the bend. The two control handles move with it.
  3. Add more dots to guide long return connections around your nodes. Use only as many as needed; each connection allows at most 64 dots.
  4. Remove a dot by right-clicking it: Windows offers Delete; the device web editor removes the dot directly. Undo restores it.

Routing dots change the drawing only. They do not create executable nodes, delays or electrical connections. Existing automatic routes remain rounded until you edit a dot manually.

Shape each side with independent Bezier handles

  1. Click an existing dot, or add a new one. A blue square controls the incoming curve and an orange square controls the outgoing curve. Incoming follows the direction from the source output to the target input, even on a wire drawn from right to left.
  2. Drag the blue square to change the incoming tangent direction and reach. The orange handle is unchanged.
  3. Drag the orange square to shape the outgoing side independently. Longer handles produce broader bends; shorter handles tighten the curve.
  4. Align both handles along the same straight axis, pointing away from the dot on opposite sides, for a smooth transition. Use different directions to make a deliberate corner. Handles are not automatically mirrored or locked together.
  5. Move the pointer along the guide line to reach a handle, or drag the dot itself to relocate the entire bend.

The curve passes through manually controlled dots. An inward curl usually means a handle points against the direction of travel: shorten it or rotate it toward the adjoining span.

Handle length limits

Each handle is limited to 10%–50% of the straight-line distance from its routing dot to the adjacent routing dot on that side, or to the element connection point when there is no intervening dot. This uses the direct distance, not the curved wire length. Incoming and outgoing limits are calculated independently. A newly enabled handle starts halfway between its original automatic reach and the 50% maximum: default = (automatic reach + 0.5 × straight-line distance) / 2. Existing manually adjusted handles keep their settings within the limits. Moving a dot or connected element recalculates the limits and clamps existing handles while preserving their direction. If both points coincide, the handle becomes zero-length until they separate again.

Move multiple selected nodes

  1. Drag a selection rectangle around the nodes, or use Ctrl to add nodes to the selection.
  2. Press and drag the header of a node that is already selected. All selected nodes move together; you do not need to keep Ctrl pressed.
  3. Click an unselected node to start a new selection. Editing a value field changes that field instead of moving nodes.

When both ends of a connection move by the same amount, its routing anchors move with them. Copying selected nodes and their internal connections also copies their routing. Handle directions remain independent, and their lengths follow the limits above.

Routing dots inside groups

Dragging an automation group also moves routing dots inside its rectangle, including dots on connections to elements outside that group. Handles are children of their dots: both move with the parent dot even when they extend outside the rectangle. A handle inside the rectangle does not pull in a dot that is outside. Resizing the rectangle changes which dots will be enclosed on the next group move; resizing itself does not move dots. Internal connections between grouped nodes keep their routing when the group moves. Undo restores the complete layout.

Undo, save and transfer to the device

  1. Use Undo and Redo for dot insertion, handle adjustments, dot movement and node movement.
  2. Save the Windows project. Compile and flash the updated firmware for the selected board to include the matching web editor. Routing metadata is carried with the Logics graph.
  3. Open the device web interface, refresh after the update, and open Logics. The same anchor and handle coordinates reproduce the route.
  4. After editing in the browser, choose Save & apply. Reload to verify persistence. Unsaved browser edits are not automatically written back into an already-open Windows project; import or reopen the updated device configuration when you need it there.

The device validates finite coordinates and complete incoming/outgoing handle pairs before accepting a graph. Its existing 32 KiB graph limit still applies, so a very dense layout can reach the limit. Reduce unnecessary routing points instead of bypassing validation.

Touch screens

A touch screen has no hover. Tap the wire or dot to enter editing, then drag a dot or handle. The selected dot and its handles remain visible until you select a different dot. Use the browser context-menu gesture on a dot only when you intend to remove it. On a computer, Shift-drag a wire keeps the existing endpoint-rewiring gesture.

Delay remains nonblocking

Delay defaults to five seconds. Connect an event output to Delay.In and Delay.Out to the required action. The ESP stores a deadline and returns to its scheduler; it does not stop the whole processor for five seconds. Other independent branches can continue to run during the wait.

A new execution pulse received by the same Delay restarts that node’s deadline rather than queuing an additional completion. Its output fires once when the deadline is reached. This is different from Repeat, which emits a configured number of pulses, and Countdown Timer, which also exposes reset, stop and remaining-time controls.

For a simple check, run two independent branches: one action directly from an event, and another through a five-second Delay. The direct action should run immediately and the delayed action later. Timed feedback loops are supported when every cycle passes through Delay, Timer, Debounce or Countdown Timer. Immediate execution loops and circular data dependencies are rejected. Repeat and Cooldown do not provide this safety barrier because they can emit immediately.

Worked example: three samples, five seconds apart

Goal: sample Wi-Fi signal strength, chip temperature and CPU load in order, changing the same built-in RGB LED to green, red and blue. Repeat until the automation is stopped. Use firmware built with timed-loop support and select the correct built-in LED type and GPIO in Configuration. A single-colour LED cannot display these three colours. Confirm that the selected chip exposes the requested measurements; an unsupported measurement should be replaced with an available numeric source.

1. Add and configure the elements

  1. Add Lifecycle · On started, three Transfer to Plotter elements, three Built-in LED elements and three Delay elements.
  2. Add Wi-Fi signal strength, chip temperature and CPU load sources. Connect each numeric output to the Value input of its corresponding Transfer to Plotter element.
  3. Name the plots Signal strength, Temperature and CPU load. Set their units to dBm, °C and % respectively.
  4. Set the first LED to RGB 0, 255, 0; the second to 255, 0, 0; and the third to 0, 0, 255. Set a suitable brightness, for example 20%, on all three. These elements operate the same physical LED.
  5. Set all three Delays to 5 seconds. Group all these elements into one automation so its Stop control stops the whole cycle.

2. Wire the execution chain

On started.Out → Signal strength.Sample now
Signal strength.Sampled → Green LED.ON
Green LED.Done → Delay 1.In
Delay 1.Out → Temperature.Sample now
Temperature.Sampled → Red LED.Set color
Red LED.Done → Delay 2.In
Delay 2.Out → CPU load.Sample now
CPU load.Sampled → Blue LED.Set color
Blue LED.Done → Delay 3.In
Delay 3.Out → Signal strength.Sample now

The first Sample now input accepts both the startup pulse and the final Delay output. Data Value inputs still take only one source. ON applies the configured green colour and turns the LED on; Set color applies red or blue and turns it on. No OFF branch is needed for a colour change. Do not connect each sample to both ON and OFF: both actions emit Done and can restart a downstream delay.

3. Check the expected timing

Elapsed timeSampleLED
0 secondsSignal strengthGreen
5 secondsTemperatureRed
10 secondsCPU loadBlue
15 secondsSignal strength againGreen
20 secondsTemperature againRed

These are nominal times measured from the startup event; scheduler and action processing can add small delays. A different parameter is sampled every five seconds, and each parameter repeats every fifteen seconds. To wait five seconds before the first sample too, place a separate five-second Delay between On started and the first Sample now input. The group Play control enables the automation; keep On started in the graph as its execution trigger.

4. Understand the connection popup

If you return directly from an action to an earlier action without a timed wait on that cycle, the connection is rejected. The popup explains why and suggests adding Delay, Timer, Debounce or Countdown to every return path with a positive duration. Correct the path, then reconnect: the valid connection is accepted. Five seconds is a useful starting value for this example. Simply increasing a timer elsewhere does not fix a path that bypasses it. Cooldown and Repeat can emit immediately, so neither alone makes that cycle valid.

A circular data dependency needs a different fix: break the data feedback path and read from an independent source. Adding Delay does not resolve circular data. Other popups explain incompatible or disabled connectors, occupied data inputs and Sampling Interval wiring. Failed rewiring preserves the original wire. Dismiss a popup with OK; the device browser also supports Escape.

5. When to use Countdown Start or Reset

The three Delays above are sufficient; do not add a repeating Timer to the same chain, which could introduce overlapping triggers. If you choose a Countdown Timer instead, return to Start after it finishes to begin another countdown. Reset restores the duration and continues only if the countdown is already running. Resetting a finished or idle countdown does not start it. Reset is useful for extending an active inactivity timeout whenever a new activity event arrives. Connecting Reset is allowed and shows an explanatory tip.

Delays yield to the ESP scheduler rather than blocking the chip. Very short intervals can still overwhelm plotting, storage or other actions. Increasing the interval reduces that workload; it does not repair incorrect wiring. Use the automation group Stop control to end the loop. Save the project and rebuild or update the device firmware before testing these new connection rules on an older installed device.
